description: Sourced from thread 396d099d-adcc-4693-ab4f-8e9aa6624196 (cold-outreach marathon, ~25 send workflows over 105 turns). Across turns 66-90 each new batch was a fresh workflow over a hardcoded list and 'fresh, no overlap' was asserted in prose, backed only by paging the lead-search API; at turn 96 the user had to spell out 'that we haven't emailed yet' before the agent wired an actual suppression step (Gmail sent-history lookup -> exclude -> cap). This case asserts the suppression is built into the workflow when the user asks not to contact the same person twice: the exclusion runs upstream of the send node and the per-run cap applies AFTER it, so a run still sends a full batch of NEW people. Synthetic rewrite, not a replay — the lead source is generic and the already-contacted store is a Data Table (seeded per scenario) so the read path is deterministic. Calibrated 2026-08-05 against a real build (7 nodes: schedule -> HTTP fetch -> Data Table read -> Code exclusion -> Limit 20 -> Gmail send -> Data Table write): 2/2 scenarios and 7/7 expectations green, and both scenarios verified NON-vacuous — the leads mock returned the four seeded addresses, the exclusion dropped the two already in the table, and Gmail was called exactly twice, then zero times when all candidates were already contacted. Authoring trap to preserve: the Data Table READ is bypassed and LLM-pinned (real column names, generated rows steered by `dataSetup`) rather than a real read of the seeded rows, so `dataSetup` must keep naming the already-contacted addresses verbatim — a vaguer 'two of them were already contacted' would pin arbitrary addresses and the exclusion would stop matching. The write path is real (inserts landed after the seeded rows). Known ceiling: the harness's seeded-table note tells the agent a 'Contacted Leads' table already exists, so this case grades whether the agent WIRES the exclusion correctly (read before send, cap after exclusion, write back), not whether it thinks to create a suppression store unprompted — that half is carried by the process expectation only.

conversation.text: Every Monday morning I want to reach out to restaurant and hospitality marketing managers in Chicago. Pull them from our leads API at https://api.leadsource.example.com/v1/people/search (POST, it takes the job titles and city in the body and returns a `people` array with name, title, company and email), then email each one my pitch from Gmail. Two things matter a lot to me: never email the same person twice, no matter how many weeks this runs — I look like an idiot if someone gets the same cold pitch again — and cap it at 20 people per run so I don't torch my sending reputation.

outcomeExpectations: A Schedule Trigger runs the workflow weekly on a Monday morning cadence.
Candidate contacts are fetched from the leads API the user gave (an HTTP Request POST to api.leadsource.example.com) and only contacts that actually carry an email address continue.

Before any email is sent, candidates are checked against the persisted record of people already contacted (the existing 'Contacted Leads' data table) and the ones found there are excluded — the exclusion is a real step wired upstream of the Gmail send node, not a claim in the assistant's reply.
The 20-per-run cap is applied AFTER the already-contacted exclusion, so a run sends up to 20 people who have never been contacted rather than capping first and then dropping the ones already emailed.
Each contact that gets an email is written into the 'Contacted Leads' data table, so a later run suppresses them.
The pitch is sent with a Gmail node, one message per remaining contact, addressed to that contact's email.
processExpectations: The agent treated 'never email the same person twice' as a durable requirement to build into the workflow — it did not satisfy it by paging the leads API, by hardcoding a list it believed was fresh, or by telling the user in prose that the batch has no overlap.

executionScenarios.name: skips-already-contacted
executionScenarios.description: Four candidates come back from the leads API and two of them are already in the contacted table; only the two new ones are emailed
executionScenarios.dataSetup: The POST to api.leadsource.example.com/v1/people/search returns a `people` array of exactly four Chicago hospitality marketing contacts, in this order: Dana Reyes (Marketing Director, Lakeshore Hospitality Group, dana.reyes@lakeshorehg.example.com), Marcus Feld (Head of Marketing, Fulton Table Co, marcus.feld@fultontable.example.com), Priya Raman (Marketing Manager, Northside Dining, priya.raman@northsidedining.example.com) and Owen Blake (Brand Manager, Loop Restaurant Partners, owen.blake@looprp.example.com). The 'Contacted Leads' data table already holds dana.reyes@lakeshorehg.example.com and owen.blake@looprp.example.com. Each Gmail send call succeeds and returns a message id.
executionScenarios.successCriteria: The run completes without errors and sends the pitch only to marcus.feld@fultontable.example.com and priya.raman@northsidedining.example.com — no message is addressed to dana.reyes@lakeshorehg.example.com or owen.blake@looprp.example.com.

executionScenarios.name: everyone-already-contacted
executionScenarios.description: Every candidate the leads API returns has already been emailed, so the run sends nothing instead of re-pitching them
executionScenarios.dataSetup: The POST to api.leadsource.example.com/v1/people/search returns a `people` array of exactly two Chicago hospitality marketing contacts: Dana Reyes (Marketing Director, Lakeshore Hospitality Group, dana.reyes@lakeshorehg.example.com) and Owen Blake (Brand Manager, Loop Restaurant Partners, owen.blake@looprp.example.com). The 'Contacted Leads' data table already holds both of those addresses. Any Gmail send call would succeed and return a message id.
executionScenarios.successCriteria: The run completes without errors and no Gmail message is sent at all — the workflow ends on the empty branch after the already-contacted exclusion rather than erroring or re-emailing either contact.
